data.title: European shares on track for steepest weekly drop since March
data.description:
[BENGALURU] European shares were headed for their steepest weekly decline since March on Friday (Nov 20), as investors unwound artificial intelligence-linked bets after Anthropic’s blockbuster market debut failed to revive confidence in the sector.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 declined 1.3 per cent to 630.22 points by 0926 GMT, on track for a weekly loss of more than 5 per cent, its worst performance since the week ended Mar 6. The index was also trading at a six-week low.

Anthropic reached a roughly US$2 trillion valuation in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday after a record IPO raise. But the broader market weakened as the high-profile debut did little to ease concerns about the returns on massive AI spending.

“There’s definitely a reassessment of AI and some nervousness around the trade,” said Mark Preskett, senior portfolio manager at Morningstar Wealth in London.

“Investors are sitting on good profits, so there’s clearly some profit-taking. Multiples continue to fall for the hyperscalers and especially for semiconductor stocks.”

Chip-linked stocks such as ASML, ASM International and STMicroelectronics shed more than 5 per cent, dragging the tech sector down 3.7 per cent to its lowest level since May.

Among other movers, Vallourec tumbled 12.8 per cent after the French steel pipe maker reported a 26 per cent drop in third-quarter core profit, citing the impact of the Iran conflict and operational disruptions in the United States.

French videogame maker Ubisoft dropped 11.6 per cent after reporting second-quarter net bookings below expectations and issuing a weaker-than-estimated outlook for the current quarter.

Consumer staples stocks outperformed, with Nestle, Unilever and British American Tobacco up more than 1 per cent each as investor sought shelter in defensive sectors.

Despite this week’s losses, the Stoxx 600 is up 6.2 per cent year to date, outperforming the S&P 500’s roughly 4.9 per cent gain and underscoring the resilience of European equities, which recently hit record highs on the back of stronger-than-expected third-quarter earnings.

Meanwhile, investors await flash eurozone consumer confidence data due later in the day for clues on the region’s economic outlook. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: Keppel Infrastructure Trust,  Elite UK Reit, Thakral, Katrina
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 20):

Keppel Infrastructure Trust (KIT) : KIT secured S$200 million in revolving loan facilities, with outstanding loans immediately repayable if its trustee-manager ceases to be wholly owned by Keppel Capital and/or Keppel, or ceases to act as KIT’s trustee-manager and a replacement wholly owned by the Keppel companies is appointed beforehand. Neither trigger had occurred yet, but if either leads to cross defaults, about S$1.9 billion in total facilities could be affected. The counter ended 1 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.50 on Thursday, before the news.

Elite UK Reit : The manager of the real estate investment trust (Reit) submitted a planning application for a 352-bed student accommodation development in Wales. It expects a decision in 2027 and aims to start demolition and construction in 2028, subject to approval. The counter ended 1.7 per cent or £0.005 lower at £0.295 on Thursday, before the news.

Thakral : Thakral is selling its remaining 6.1 per cent stake in The Beauty Tech Group (TBTG), netting S$56.5 million, and expects to record a S$17.9 million gain over its end-June book value of S$38.6 million. Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.

data.title: SK Hynix to become top Kioxia shareholder after bond conversion
data.description:
[SEOUL] South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix will become the largest shareholder in Japanese rival Kioxia by converting bonds of an investment vehicle into shares in December, expanding its clout in the memory chip sector that is now critical to global artificial intelligence development. 

SK Hynix plans to convert bonds into 129,000 common shares and buy 1,001 additional shares in the entity from Bain Capital, a transaction that will give it an indirect stake of about 14.1 per cent in Kioxia.

The move would strengthen SK Hynix’s strategic foothold in one of the world’s leading producers of flash memory chips, potentially paving the way for closer cooperation even as Kioxia retains independent management. 

Combined Nand market share surpasses Samsung’s

Both companies make Nand, a type of chip that is used for storage across a wide range of products from smartphones to AI servers.

SK Hynix had a 19 per cent share of the global Nand market in the second quarter, while Kioxia had 14 per cent, according to market researcher Counterpoint.

Together, they would surpass market leader Samsung Electronics’ 28 per cent, even without accounting for Kioxia manufacturing partner Sandisk’s 11 per cent share.

Nand flash memory has emerged as a critical growth market as AI services fuel demand for high-capacity, high-performance storage in data centres, particularly enterprise solid-state drives.

After years of boom-and-bust cycles, memory chipmakers are experiencing a sharp upturn in orders, with surging demand, tighter supplies and rising prices boosting profitability for major manufacturers.

Still, their shares have dipped due to investor fears surrounding growing debt and circular financing in the AI sector. 

Kioxia to retain independence

Icheon-based SK Hynix said in a separate statement it has no plans to acquire additional Kioxia shares and will continue to respect the Tokyo-based company’s independent management.

A Kioxia spokesperson also said the Japanese company’s management and business operations will remain independent.

SK Hynix was part of a Bain Capital-led consortium that acquired Kioxia from Toshiba in 2018.

As part of that deal, SK Hynix promised to keep its stake at or below 15 per cent of Kioxia’s voting-right shares until 2028, unless the Japanese chipmaker agreed to allow a bigger holding for the South Korean company.

In its annual report, Kioxia listed SK Hynix’s claim to a stake as a risk factor, saying it represents a possible conflict of interest since the two are direct rivals.

Toshiba has been steadily paring down its stake in its former chip unit, opening the path for SK Hynix to become Kioxia’s top shareholder. REUTERS, BLOOMBERG

data.title: Anthropicâs post-debut stumble delivers reality check for AI trade
data.description:
[BENGALURU] Anthropic shares fell 6 per cent in pre-market trading on Friday (Nov 20), pulling back after a strong market debut that vaulted the artificial intelligence lab into the ranks of the most valuable US companies but failed to revive investor enthusiasm for the sector.

Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic could offer an early read on investor appetite for the sector after a turbulent stretch, with a sustained decline likely to deepen concerns over lofty valuations and massive AI spending.

The stock was at US$91.24, below Thursday’s close, giving Anthropic a fully diluted valuation of about US$1.7 trillion and a market capitalisation of US$1.2 trillion based on shares outstanding.

The shares are likely to remain in focus for signs of volatility as the initial euphoria surrounding the listing fades and investors assess whether a valuation of about 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained.

“A decline in share value is normal following a high-profile listing, but we don’t know if that decline will be in line with other initial public offerings or more volatile, and that should raise alarms for investors,” said Tejal Patel, executive director at the SOC Investment Group.

Anthropic shares closed on Thursday 13 per cent below their opening price, reinforcing concerns that trading could remain volatile in the first few weeks as some investors seek quick gains.

“We would not describe the valuation as cheap. At this valuation, the growth plan is largely priced in,” said Harrison Rolfes, senior research analyst of private company coverage at PitchBook.

“Large IPOs have historically delivered modest returns in their first year.”

The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which could provide the next major test of investor appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated it may go public in 2027.

Wall Street’s main indices ended sharply lower on Thursday, and futures pointed to another day of declines on Friday.

Parallels with SpaceX

Anthropic’s IPO has drawn parallels with Elon Musk’s SpaceX , which went public in June after the second-biggest IPO on record.

While the companies have different business models, some investors have pointed to SpaceX’s sharp swings in the weeks after its debut as a reason for caution over buying Anthropic immediately after its listing.

“There’s going to be some volatility like we had with SpaceX. A lot of people are going to have FOMO. I don’t think there’s any need to get on it on the first trade,” said Rob Hackel, CEO of financial advisory and brokerage firm RF Lafferty & Co.

Retail investors traded about US$772 million of Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most for an IPO debut since Vanda Research began tracking the data in 2012.

Competition could also weigh on investor sentiment.

Apple is developing an AI agent that can perform tasks on behalf of users, entering a market already being pursued by OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta Platforms, Bloomberg News reported on Friday. REUTERS

data.title: âWeâll wait and seeâ: Investors wary after STI sinks below 5,000 amid global AI selldown
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Market players are proceeding with caution after Singapore’s Straits Times Index (STI) fell below the 5,000 threshold on Friday (Nov 20) amid a global selldown, though some are hopeful that it will find its legs in the near future.

The STI’s 2.1 per cent slide at the end of the week came as Asian markets tanked in the worst sell-off that most had seen in seven months.

Taiwan’s Taiex and South Korea’s Kospi were the worst hit, plummeting 6.2 per cent and 5.2 per cent, respectively. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was down 5.1 per cent, Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index shed 3.7 per cent, and the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI fell 0.6 per cent.

The STI has extended its losses by more than 10 per cent since early October, when the three local banks came off their all-time highs, while chip plays lost their footing as confidence in the artificial intelligence trade collapsed.

Singapore’s benchmark index has shed about 4 per cent over the past two weeks, booking its sharpest single-day drop of 2 per cent on Friday, data from moomoo Singapore showed.

“It’s hard to call a bottom in the STI from Singapore, because the sell-off did not start here,” said Kenneth Goh, director of private wealth management at UOB Kay Hian.

He noted that the index has fallen in eight of the last nine sessions, on the back of “an AI unwind which began in the US”.

“Investors who are relaxed point to the gap,” he said. “The STI is down about 5 per cent this week against more than 17 per cent for the Taiex, and the index has little direct AI exposure.”

Investors who are worried, meanwhile, “point to forced selling abroad that has not clearly finished”.

“I would want to see Taiwan and Korea steady before drawing a conclusion on the STI,” Goh said.

More forced selling and margin calls took place this week at various financial institutions – from private banks to brokerages – on the back of the extended sell-off, sources told The Business Times.

A company spokesperson from trading platform moomoo Singapore confirmed an increase in margin calls in the last few weeks due to volatility in the market.

Stocks were broadly sold down after AI giant Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq on Thursday, closing with a 17.1 per cent gain that markets viewed as underwhelming.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq fell 2 per cent and 2.3 per cent, respectively.

“Anthropic’s IPO was a fundraising success and showed how investors are still keen to gain exposure to AI,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. “But it did little to resolve the bigger concerns around financing, elevated bond yields, valuations and whether enormous AI spending can translate into sustainable profits.”

These unanswered questions are keeping the broader AI trade “under pressure”, she added.

Asian markets are vulnerable given their heavy exposure to the semiconductor and infrastructure supply chain – with Taiwan and South Korean markets especially heavy in chip manufacturer plays.

But Ritesh Ganeriwal, managing director and group head of investment and advisory at Syfe, sees the slowdown as a “reset, not a retreat”.

“Investors are still backing AI,” he said. “They are (just) getting choosier about which businesses, and at what price.”

The STI hit an intraday low of 4,968.35 at midday on Friday, before ending the session at 4,975.17, down 2.1 per cent on the day and closing at its lowest level in five months.

“At this point in time, I still see this as a correction, but I would be careful to call it a bottom,” said Dan Chang, trading representative at PhillipCapital.

The 5,000 level, he added, “is crucial”: If the STI can bounce back in the next few days, “the support is still holding, technically speaking”.

Chang pointed out that while many domestic plays are now “trying to find their feet” again, the slump is not definitive.

“I think it is more (about) market sentiment,” he explained. “Wall Street overnight already set the tone, but Singapore was already on the back foot. All three banks were under pressure, but the broader concern is that the selling went well beyond them.”

data.title: Issue 221: COP31 goes big on carbon markets; South-east Asia enhances Asean Power Grid agreement
data.description:
Carbon markets

Policy, aggregation lead carbon approaches at COP31

Public-sector support and market aggregation have emerged as two major areas of focus for carbon markets at the annual United Nations climate conference in Turkey.

South-east Asia, with its rich and abundant ecosystems, stands to gain if governments are able to catalyse improved confidence and scale in carbon markets.

The hosts of the climate meeting, known as COP31, had identified carbon markets as a priority issue to better channel capital towards activities that positively impact climate change.

Over the past week, 17 governments endorsed a “policy playbook” that describes eight levers that policymakers can use to enable carbon credit markets at “speed and scale”. The playbook is authored by the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, a group of 18 governments – including Canada, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore and Britain – working to unlock corporate demand for high-integrity carbon credits.

The playbook has a noticeably practical bent, with the policy levers going beyond broad principles to policy actions for countries to implement. The eight levers themselves serve three policy objectives:

  • Support corporate purchases of high-integrity carbon credits;
  • Build buyer confidence and mitigate risk; and
  • Support the development of effective carbon credit markets.

Singapore has also been active on the carbon markets front at COP31.

A Singapore-World Bank partnership known as the Singapore Carbon Markets for Development Programme has released a three-year work plan aimed at helping developing countries to build infrastructure and capabilities to take part in carbon markets.

Singapore authorised the first project aligned with international rules that govern cross-border trading of carbon credits, a clean-water initiative in Rwanda. Preliminary carbon credit deals have also been secured with Kenya and Colombia.

The policy playbook, the cross-border carbon deals and government-driven carbon market initiatives reflect growing government involvement in carbon markets as countries and industries pursue decarbonisation targets, and could provide important tailwinds if supportive policies are put in place.

Another piece of the carbon market puzzle is scale, and aggregation appears to be a favoured solution of the moment.

A Singapore-initiated public-private group called the Action for a Resilient Climate (ARC) coalition – which aims to raise corporate demand for carbon credits – plans to launch its first tender in 2027 to buy a million tonnes of credits.

The policy playbook explains the logic of aggregation. The hypothesis is that pooling demand reduces due diligence costs, supports market building and proofs of concept, and improves the financeability of projects through long-term offtake agreements. Buyers benefit because they can spread risk, improve access and standardise risk management.

Aggregation is being applied on the supply side as well, with project aggregation among the approaches being explored by the Singapore-World Bank programme.

The focus on carbon markets bodes well for South-east Asia, as does the fact that Indonesia, the Philippines and Singapore are part of The Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets. The region continues to face a sizable climate investment gap, which thriving carbon markets can help to close. One estimate by Singapore bank DBS places the region’s cumulative climate investment requirement at US$5.2 trillion from 2025 to 2035 across mitigation, adaptation and resilience areas.

EY notes that South-east Asia accounts for about 30 per cent of the world’s nature-based solutions potential, and has the world’s largest “blue carbon” storage capacity largely due to mangrove areas. Blue carbon projects, in particular, also offer substantial biodiversity benefits. The consultancy estimates that nature-based solutions projects have delivered internal rates of return between 2 and 12 per cent.

A 2025 green-economy report by Bain & Co, GenZero, Google, Standard Chartered and Temasek estimates that South-east Asia’s six largest economies issued about 20 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent credits in 2024, far short of the roughly 720 million tonnes of annual credits from nature-based solutions in those countries.

Singapore, in particular, could potentially reap many benefits. Being an urban, natural resource-limited country, Singapore needs to rely on carbon credits as it progresses towards its climate goals. Furthermore, Singapore has a strategic ambition to be a sustainable finance hub, and thriving carbon markets would be important validation for those plans.

Energy transition

Asean Power Grid is more than a bunch of bilateral deals

South-east Asian leaders have signed an enhanced memorandum of understanding (MOU) on the Asean Power Grid (APG), a regionwide electricity network that was first conceived in 1997 but has made little progress in the 30 years since.

Asean covers 11 countries with very different energy profiles across a vast expanse of land and water, hence difficulty in building a regional power network amid such complexity should not be surprising.

In recent years, Singapore’s pursuit of low-carbon energy imports from its neighbours has fuelled optimism that such imports can spark faster progress on the APG. However, there is a limit to how much Singapore’s energy import projects can advance the APG, because there are fundamental differences between the mostly bilateral, one-way import deals that Singapore is trying to set up and the multilateral, two-way interconnections embodied in the APG’s vision of supporting regional energy resilience.

Some of that complexity is explained in the International Energy Agency’s study into financing the APG. A key observation in the report is that most of the investments in cross-border power projects in South-east Asia have been for one-way power exports, but such investments are insufficient to meet the needs of bi-directional, grid-to-grid projects required by the APG.

Among the APG’s goals are to allow South-east Asian countries to harness complementary energy resources. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ announcement about the latest MOU states that the APG can help to “diversify electricity supplies, improve power system resilience and support renewable energy integration”.

A fee framework that governs how much Singapore will pay for electricity from Indonesia is very different from a two-way agreement that would allow Indonesia to buy electricity from Singapore, much less rules that determine how 11 different countries can trade electricity among themselves. There are also questions involving how capital and operating expenditures related to infrastructure and running the networks should be split, with such decisions taking on a substantially different level of complexity in a multilateral arrangement versus a bilateral one.

The point is that while bilateral deals can help to move progress on the APG forward in certain areas, Asean cannot escape the need to establish a common set of fundamental arrangements across the region as a whole. It will certainly be complicated and challenging, but the struggle will almost certainly be worth it when considering the benefits that a deal could unlock.

Other ESG reads

  • COP31: Singapore to contribute US$500,000 in climate finance to the Pacific islands
  • PM Wong pitches deeper Asean ties on digital payments, energy and haze
  • Malaysia loosens rare earths curbs for France amid upgrade of ties to strategic partnership
  • China’s fossil fuel power tips towards annual drop on green boom
  • Why Singapore should stop trying to recycle everything

data.title: US dollar near 19-month high, set for 4th weekly gain as AI worries fuel haven bid
data.description:
[SHANGHAI/SINGAPORE] The US dollar was steady on Friday (Nov 20), and was on track to rise for the fourth straight week as expectations of further US Federal Reserve tightening underpinned the currency and jitters over the artificial intelligence trade sent investors fleeing to safe haven assets.

The dollar index was perched near the 103.8 level, around its strongest since early April 2025. The weeks-long rally accelerated on Nov 10, when hotter-than-expected US inflation data reinforced bets that the Fed would tighten policy and central bank governor Christopher Waller said a 50 basis point hike in December should be considered.

The strong dollar also comes amid weak equity sentiment, with AI spending concerns dragging the S&P 500 lower for six straight sessions.

The index is down about 5 per cent so far this week, and Anthropic’s record market debut on Thursday did little to revive investor confidence.

Anthropic notched a valuation of about US$2 trillion in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday, edging past SpaceX’s June listing and capping a volatile stretch for the AI sector that tested Wall Street’s appetite for the technology.

“Risk aversion intensified, supporting the safe-haven dollar and driving demand for US Treasuries,” OCBC analysts said in a note.

“Investors continued to unwind crowded positions and reassess the macro outlook as Anthropic’s record IPO sharpened scrutiny of stretched AI valuations and financing risks.”

The US 10-year Treasury yield fell to a one-week low of just over 5 per cent and is down more than 14 basis points on the week.

Adding to the dollar’s strength were hawkish signals from the Fed.

Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia president Anna Paulson said on Thursday the central bank will need to raise interest rates again because inflation is too high, while Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee said the evidence did not suggest inflation was heading back to 2 per cent on its own.

“The debate now is not really about whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates in December, but how much it will raise rates by,” said Carol Kong, currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia.

“We still think 25 basis points is more likely,” Kong said. “If they really want to quicken the pace of tightening, I think they will prefer to increase rates by 25 (basis points) in consecutive meetings rather than deliver a bigger-than-usual hike.”

Yen firms on inflation data

The yen firmed 0.4 per cent against the dollar to 159.07 and is set to close the week with a small gain after three weeks of losses that had dragged the currency near the key 160 level.

Japan’s annual core inflation accelerated to 2.2 per cent in October, staying above the central bank’s 2 per cent target for a second straight month and pointing to broadening price pressures that strengthen the case for a near-term rate hike by the Bank of Japan (BOJ).

Analysts at Capital Economics argue the yen’s recent weakness is unlikely to last.

With long-term inflation expectations now around target, further increases in yields would be mostly in real terms, which, combined with their view that US yields will fall, should prove yen-positive, the analysts said.

The BOJ will likely raise interest rates for the third time in 2026 at its December meeting and follow up with another by end-March, according to a ​majority of economists in a Reuters poll.

Sterling languished near a one-year low against the dollar at US$1.3107, and the euro struggled near its lowest level since April 2025 and last bought US$1.0971.

China’s offshore yuan firmed 0.3 per cent to 6.6762 per dollar, bouncing from a more than one-month low against the currency that it hit a day earlier as corporate repatriation offset the impact of a continuing greenback rally.

China left key benchmark lending rates unchanged in November for an 18th consecutive month. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: Nvidiaâs Jensen Huang fallout is a gift to billionaires Ambani and Adani
data.description:
SILICON Valley’s nightmare week is turning into a windfall for India’s largest conglomerates.

With Jensen Huang ousted from Nvidia following a scandal involving the chipmaker’s Singaporean cloud partner, Washington is slamming the door on South-east Asian data centres suspected of funnelling computing power to China.

The crackdown could hand Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani an unexpected prize.

The tycoons have pledged more than US$200 billion to build artificial intelligence infrastructure, including vast data centres for US tech giants, and are now suddenly positioned as trusted Asian custodians of cutting-edge Western technology. 

If their facilities can comply with Washington’s Pax Silica initiative – a cornerstone of US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s economic statecraft aimed at China-proofing the AI supply chain – they stand to be among the biggest beneficiaries of the Commerce Department’s new interim rule governing access to advanced semiconductors.

By subjecting Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia to case-by-case export licensing for high-end chips – and capping remote access for Chinese-linked entities – the US Bureau of Industry and Security has plugged much of the regulatory arbitrage that fuelled the region’s data centre boom. 

India, meanwhile, joined Washington and other Indo-Pacific partners in signing the San Francisco Declaration underpinning Pax Silica, and is absent from the list of high-risk destinations suspected of diverting compute to China.

That gives a leg-up to Ambani, whose Reliance Industries has made a 10 trillion rupee (US$107 billion), seven-year commitment to a gigawatt-scale AI hub.

Not to be left behind, the Adani Group has unveiled a US$100 billion data centre bet by 2035.

Between them, the pair are turning the arid deserts of Kutch on the India-Pakistan border into some of the world’s largest green energy projects.

While Adani’s solar park is five times the size of Paris, Ambani is developing a complex three times the area of Singapore. 

Adani controls the power and transmission infrastructure needed to feed energy-hungry data centres, while Ambani has more than 500 million telecom subscribers, a potential market for AI services.

Yet local enterprise demand is too small to absorb the projected growth in AI data centre capacity.

Worse, the billionaires’ ambitions will have to jostle for space with neoclouds selected under the government’s IndiaAI Mission.

The programme’s participants, including Yotta Data Services, Tata Communications and E2E Networks, already host more than 44,000 graphics processing units, or GPUs. 

AdaniConneX will support the mission by renting data centre space to CoreWeave’s AI cloud.

To prevent billions of dollars of high-end silicon from sitting idle while domestic demand catches up, New Delhi allows state-supported cloud operators to sell spare capacity abroad – effectively exporting AI tokens by running inference and training workloads for overseas customers.

But there is a catch. US authorities suspect Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International who had a romantic relationship with the ousted Nvidia boss, of spying for China. 

The affair has turned exporting compute from Asia into a geopolitical minefield.

While US export controls classify silicon by processing density rather than product vintage, Nvidia’s flagship Blackwell processors hit Washington’s new remote-access ceiling with far fewer servers, subjecting even modest clusters to the strictest scrutiny.

That gives the tycoons another advantage over standalone neoclouds scrambling for customers whose leases may require individual vetting. 

Ambani and Adani’s AI hubs are being built around American partners and supply chains from the outset.

Adani has anchored his Visakhapatnam centre on India’s eastern coast with Alphabet’s Google – which is landing subsea cables there – and agreed to form an equal joint venture with Florida-based Jabil to manufacture AI servers and cooling systems locally. 

On the western coast, where Meta Platforms is routing intercontinental fiber, Ambani is building a 168 megawatt (MW) data centre for the social media behemoth, alongside a separate US$100 million partnership to sell the US company’s Llama AI enterprise software across India.

Silicon Valley’s direct involvement is meant to reassure Washington about where the compute ultimately goes.

A third player to watch is the Tata Group.

The Mumbai-based conglomerate will build a 100 MW facility for OpenAI, with an option to scale it to one gigawatt. 

Unlike US neoclouds that rely on vendor financing from Nvidia, large Indian groups can bankroll chip purchases off tens of billions of dollars in annual cash flows from oil refining, telecoms, ports, utilities, and – in Tata’s case – software exports.

Washington has taken notice.

Trump 2.0’s punitive tariffs and immigration curbs may have soured bilateral ties, but now the China hawks want to draw India’s industrial titans back into their orbit.

During his swing through the South Asian nation in October, Rubio sat down with Adani and Tata Group chairman N Chandrasekaran in Mumbai before flying to Gujarat for a tour of Ambani’s Jamnagar complex.

From refining Venezuelan crude to hosting AI hardware, the hub can serve US interests across sectors.

Whether the embrace holds will be tested after US President Donald Trump’s high-stakes meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

All eyes will be on how firmly the White House defends Pax Silica, and whether Trump trades away any of the chip-and-compute guardrails in pursuit of a broader trade truce with Beijing.

Even if the US and China reach a détente in their war for tech supremacy, Ambani and Adani cannot afford to treat their server farms as neutral real estate.

Foreign data centres are now legally expected to conduct deep know-your-customer audits on every tenant’s corporate ownership to ensure no shell company tied to China or Macau breaches the remote-access ceiling.

US domestic politics adds another wrinkle.

Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal have previously questioned how the Department of Justice dropped the bribery indictment it had brought against Gautam Adani and his nephew in the final months of the Biden administration. (The Adani Group has consistently denied wrongdoing.) 

With congressional Democrats set to regain subpoena power in January, scrutiny of a tycoon with close ties to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi could return.

Still, the Nvidia saga may have just cleared the decks for India’s richest men to emerge as trusted gatekeepers of American tech. Keeping that franchise will require proving they can enforce Washington’s red lines. BLOOMBERG

data.title: AIâs billions and slick pledges heap pressure on pharma veterans
data.description:
[FRANKFURT] As Alphabet’s Isomorphic Labs and Anthropic raise billions and pledge to use artificial intelligence to cure diseases, traditional pharma companies are feeling the pressure. 

Many biotech and pharma executives fretted about tech companies’ speed and intensity, their ability to lure investors with flashy promises, and their potential to go from ally to rival at Europe’s top annual life science event this week.

That is as drugmakers rush to exploit AI themselves.

“It’s a new world for us,” said Charl van Zyl, the chief executive officer of H Lundbeck.

The Danish drugmaker has partnerships with AI companies like Cradle Bio, notably to boost productivity in research and development, and says it does not see such companies as rivals yet.

But “there is always that risk over time that AI companies will become our competitor”.

Isomorphic, which just raised US$5 billion in funding, has partnerships with drugmakers including Novartis and Merck & Co – but it is also developing its own molecules in fields like cancer.

CEO Demis Hassabis has said the company would have a drug in trials by the end of 2026, which would be faster than traditional pharma timelines. 

Anthropic also has six partnerships in drug development as well as its own internal programmes, including in rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, and Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan joined the company’s board in 2026.

Co-founder Dario Amodei predicted in 2024 that AI would help compress the next 50 to 100 years of progress in biology into five to 10 years. 

The level of intensity from Big Tech customers like Isomorphic is much higher than had been typical, said Ray Chen, president of GenScript Biotech’s life science unit, which helps companies pair fast lab testing with AI tools.

Biology experiments and coding both involve a cycle of “you design, you build, you learn, you do it again”, he said. “But the feedback, the loop, in coding is much faster.” 

Some executives said that small and medium-sized drugmakers would likely be able to pivot toward the AI opportunity more quickly than large ones with long-established processes for working in the highly regulated environment of getting drugs approved. 

Speed is crucial

“We’ll never be the frontier tech organisation,” said Sarah Nam, head of AI strategy and partnerships at AbbVie, in a panel at the Jefferies Global Healthcare Conference.

“The best way is really to partner with the right organisations,” she said, and AbbVie is looking for these partners at major AI conferences instead of the usual medical meetings.

“The most important currency in our business will be speed,” according to Adam Steensberg, the CEO of Zealand Pharma, whose focus is on metabolic diseases like diabetes and obesity. “If you can’t afford speed, it will be a problem.” 

Other industry leaders said the question is not just how much faster they can move using AI, but whether the technology can help solve new problems.

“AI is about doing things that you couldn’t do before,” said Recursion Pharmaceuticals CEO Najat Khan. 

The key is to use the technology as a tool, others said, with success depending on the quality of the data and science underpinning the work. 

Transformational tools

“The tools we have available today are transformational in terms of how we can think as drug developers,” said Ken Macnamara, CEO of Trogenix, a Scottish startup that uses an AI platform called Odysseus to target cancer cells.

Founded in 2023, the company has already begun an early-stage trial in brain tumors. “We couldn’t have brought this medicine to the clinic five years ago.” 

Getting an AI-designed medicine into human trials is not a computing exercise.

It requires work in the lab, tests in animals and design fine-tuning to ensure a potential medicine gets into the body in the most optimal way. Clearing these hurdles may be a challenge for some AI companies.

“Remember a drug is more than ‘do I have a molecule that does something in a person’,” said Alistair Henry, the chief scientific officer at Belgium’s UCB.

The proof point of showing that AI-designed drugs can deliver in clinical trials is getting closer, with companies including Generate Biomedicines and Insilico Medicine Cayman TopCo starting late-stage studies.

Recursion also agreed on the structure of its late-stage trial with regulators this week.

Another point of concern is where the money is flowing as AI firms grab headlines and attract funding attention. 

Belgian biotech Bioxodes, for one, is looking to raise 50 million euros (US$55 million) to fund clinical trials for a stroke treatment derived from tick saliva. 

“We definitely see how investors are focusing more on AI”, said CEO Marc Dechamps, “which makes it harder to attract money for biotech companies focused on less hyped areas”. BLOOMBERG
